name: Orthodontic headgear and facemask

card.summary: Strap-on orthodontic force appliance for kids' bite and jaw growth; adult facial-change claims lack support.
card.note: Compliance-dependent; eye-injury and airway concerns reported.

quick.overview:
Headgear and facemasks apply outside-the-mouth force to guide jaw growth and correct bites in children, with the facemask pulling the upper jaw forward for underbites.
Trials support use in growing patients. Looksmaxxing claims of forward maxillary growth in adults are not backed by evidence.
quick.mechanism: Straps anchor to the head or neck, and elastics or a frame transmit force to the teeth and jaw, restraining or advancing the upper jaw.
quick.risks: Eye injuries, tooth soreness, social stigma and possible airway or facial-growth effects are reported; effectiveness depends on many hours of daily wear.

lead: Orthodontic headgear is an appliance worn partly outside the mouth, anchored by straps to the head or neck, that applies force to the teeth or jaws to correct the bite and guide growth, mainly in children [1]. For appearance, its purpose is to change how the upper and lower jaws relate to each other: restraining a protruding upper jaw, pulling back upper teeth, or, with the reverse-pull headgear or facemask, bringing a recessed upper jaw forward so that the profile and the bite line up [1][2].

The facemask is the best-known variant in appearance circles. A frame rests on the forehead and chin, and elastics run from the frame to an appliance in the mouth, applying a forward pull on the upper jaw. The Cochrane review of orthodontic treatment for Class III malocclusion (underbite) in children describes the facemask as the most commonly reported non-surgical intervention, usually attached to an expansion appliance [2]. Controlled trials in children aged roughly 5 to 13 report more forward movement of the upper jaw and a corrected bite right after treatment compared with no treatment [2][11].

In looksmaxxing communities the device is discussed under names such as facepuller or face mask, usually alongside palatal expansion (MARPE or MSE) as a non-surgical route to a more forward midface. Published trial evidence concerns children and young adolescents; forum members debate how much of it carries over to older teens and adults, and some build or discuss homemade versions [6][7][16][17].

chain: Straps anchor to the head and elastics pull on the upper jaw
The upper jaw is guided forward or restrained while it is still growing
A more balanced profile and corrected bite
angle.text: In children and young adolescents, headgear and facemasks are used to change how far forward the upper jaw sits relative to the lower jaw, which changes the profile and the bite. People in looksmaxxing communities ask whether the same approach, often paired with a palatal expander, can move a recessed maxilla forward after growth has slowed.

paras: Headgear has three working parts: a facebow or J-hooks that connect to molar tubes or braces, a headcap or strap that goes around the head or neck, and elastics or springs that link the two and supply the force [1]. Standard facebow headgear mainly pulls the upper molars back or restrains growth of the upper jaw; cervical (neck-strap) and high-pull designs change the direction of that pull; a headgear helmet covers the entire head with a cap or rigid shell; and the reverse-pull facemask pulls the upper jaw forward [1].

A facemask has a frame supported by a chin cup and a forehead pad, plus a mouth yoke that carries elastics; up to six elastics can be used to apply forward and sideways forces [1]. It is commonly paired with a rapid palatal expander, and headgear in general is used with braces, expanders and functional appliances such as the Herbst appliance and twin blocks [1][2].

Purposes listed include correcting protruding upper teeth, treating underbites and making space for crowded teeth [1]. For looks, the relevant uses are those that change jaw relationship: a Class II protrusion treated by restraining the upper jaw, or a Class III underbite treated by advancing it [1][2].

Prescribed wear ranges from 12 to 23 hours a day, with 14 to 16 hours common, and treatment typically lasts 12 to 18 months depending on severity, wear and growth stage [1]. Because daytime wear is hard to keep up, headgear is often worn in the evening and during sleep [1]. A review of temporary anchorage devices notes that extraoral headgear suffers from patient-compliance problems [5], and a 1981 study examined orthodontic cooperation, including headgear wear, with psychological measures [4].

Class III malocclusion, in which the lower teeth sit in front of the upper teeth, affects between 5 and 15 percent of populations in one systematic review [11]. A review of developing Class III malocclusions describes it as a growth-related deformity with a multifactorial cause in which inherited and environmental factors interact, and as a condition whose diagnosis is challenging in growing children because the upper jaw, lower jaw, cranial base and vertical or transverse dimensions can each contribute [14].

Timing is central. Early intervention, roughly ages 7 to 13, is described as a way to influence growth while it is still under way and possibly avoid later surgery, and adolescents are reported to adapt quickly, while adults are prescribed headgear less often [1]. The question of how long early changes last and whether they replace later jaw surgery is a main subject of the trials below [2][12].
A randomised two-phase trial of early Class II treatment reported favourable growth changes in about 75% of children treated early with a headgear or a functional appliance [3].

For underbites, a 2017 systematic review and meta-analysis of early Class III treatment included 15 studies (9 randomised and 6 non-randomised controlled trials) in children aged 7 to 12; only three of the randomised trials had a low risk of bias. Three randomised trials with 141 participants compared a protraction facemask with no treatment and found significantly greater correction of reverse overjet and of the ANB angle (a measure of the relationship of the upper jaw to the lower). The authors rated the evidence for short-term skeletal and dental benefit as moderate and described long-term benefit as unproven [11]. A second systematic review of facemask therapy with or without palatal expansion (22 articles, 8 in the cephalometric meta-analysis) found a positive effect on forward development of the upper jaw that was not mainly driven by expansion, with more dental side effects when no expansion was used [13].

The 2024 Cochrane review (29 trials, 1,169 children aged 5 to 13, all at high risk of bias) found moderate-certainty improvements in overjet and jaw relationship immediately after non-surgical treatment compared with untreated controls. In a single facemask study the benefits had shrunk by three years and were no longer detectable at six years, although clinicians judged treated children less likely to need jaw surgery later. No treatment clearly outperformed the facemask, and adding rapid maxillary expansion or surgical anchorage gave little or no extra benefit [2].

A UK multicentre randomised trial followed 73 children aged 7 to 9 for six years. A panel judged that 36 percent of the facemask group and 66 percent of controls needed orthognathic surgery (P = 0.027; odds ratio 3.34). Skeletal and occlusal improvement, self-esteem and appearance-related measures did not differ significantly between groups, and the authors noted that the surgery-avoidance effect was not explained by maintained skeletal change on cephalometric measures [12].

Research since the late 2000s has examined anchoring protraction to bone rather than teeth. Pilot and single-group studies using miniplates reported forward movement of the upper jaw of around 3.7 millimetres over a year in 9 to 13 year-olds, and skeletal improvement with little dental effect in a six-patient pilot [15]. A study of 15 late adolescents measured opening of the mid-palatal and pterygopalatine sutures with a micro-implant-supported skeletal expander [15]. Looksmaxxing discussions of MARPE and MSE with a facemask draw on this skeletal-anchorage literature, while the trials themselves enrolled children and young adolescents.

Common effects are tooth soreness when chewing or when the teeth touch, restrictions on eating and some activities (a straw is suggested for drinks with a facemask), and social stigma or teasing among teenagers [1]. Eye injuries have been reported, including in a 1985 ophthalmology study, and safety facebows and release straps are designed to reduce the risk [1].

A 2006 review by Nanda and Dandajena reported that long-term use may flatten the face, restrict chin and jaw growth and reduce measured SNA and ANB angles, which Wikipedia links to a smaller airway; in the 1980s some patients reported sleep apnea, breathing difficulty and acute temporomandibular disorder, and that article marks the claim as needing further explanation [1]. Wikipedia also notes that headgear use has declined in some practices because mini-implants can achieve similar tooth movements, though it remains widely used [1].

On looksmax.org, the facemask appears mainly in threads about a recessed maxilla. Posters ask whether a facemask can fix a recessed upper jaw and whether it is safe, in one case attributing the recession to keeping only the tongue tip on the palate [20]. Others ask how many millimetres of forward growth to expect at age 20 [7], whether MARPE plus a facemask is worthwhile for a narrow palate and a recessed maxilla at 18 [6], and whether to add a chin cup after expansion [19]. Replies vary, from posters who tell an 18-year-old that the results would be negligible and suggest saving for jaw surgery [6] to members who treat the device as worth trying.

A separate strand covers do-it-yourself builds: threads describe a homemade facepuller device, a helmet-style facepuller and ideas for a counter-clockwise-rotation design [16][17][18]. Members also ask about adding growth hormone, peptides or other compounds to improve facemask and expander outcomes [9][10]; no published study tests such combinations. A further thread asks why people who believe in mewing do not wear a face mask, linking the two approaches to the same goal of a more forward midface [21].

Trials and reviews concern children: the Class II headgear trial [3], the Class III facemask reviews and the Cochrane review [2][11][13], the six-year surgery-avoidance trial [12], bone-anchored protraction studies [15], and compliance research [4][5]. No studies found of facemask treatment for aesthetic purposes in adults.

timeline.event: A study examines orthodontic cooperation, including headgear wear, with psychological measures [4].
A study in Archives of Ophthalmology documents eye injuries associated with headgear [1].
Some patients report breathing problems and jaw-joint disorders after headgear, prompting controversy [1].
A 20-patient study reports positive overjet in all patients after 6 to 9 months of facemask and expansion, with 15 of 20 maintaining it at 4 years [15].
A two-phase randomised trial of early Class II treatment reports favourable growth in about 75% of early-treated children [3].
A randomised trial of 46 children compares facemask with and without expansion; both treated groups improved by close to 4 degrees ANB [15].
A review by Nanda and Dandajena reports long-term headgear use may flatten the face and restrict chin growth [1].
A CBCT study of 25 children reports about 3.7 mm forward movement of the upper jaw with bone-anchored maxillary protraction [15].
A systematic review of facemask with or without expansion concludes facemask therapy advances the maxilla [13].
Six-year follow-up of a UK randomised trial finds fewer treated children judged to need jaw surgery (36% vs 66%) [12].
A systematic review of early Class III treatment rates short-term facemask benefit as moderate [11].
A Cochrane review of 29 trials finds benefits at the end of treatment but uncertainty about lasting effects [2].

lore.intro: Headgear and facemasks are discussed on looksmax.org as a non-surgical way to advance a recessed maxilla, often combined with palatal expansion, and sometimes built at home.

claims.claim: MARPE plus a facemask can produce forward maxillary growth even in older teens
claims.believers: Posters ask how many millimetres of forward growth to expect from a facemask at 20 and whether MARPE with a facemask is good value for a recessed maxilla [6][7].
claims.experts: Published facemask evidence concerns children and adolescents with Class III malocclusion [2][11]; critics on the same forum argue such treatment gives negligible results past adolescence [6][8].

claims.claim: Growth-hormone or peptide compounds can enhance headgear or facemask results
claims.believers: A poster planning MARPE and a facemask asked which compounds to use, and a teenager asked about adding GH [9][10].
claims.experts: No published studies test hormones or peptides alongside orthodontic headgear.

claims.claim: A recessed maxilla caused by tongue posture can be pulled forward with a facemask
claims.believers: An original poster attributes a recessed upper jaw to resting only the tongue tip on the palate and asks whether a facemask will fix it [20].
claims.experts: Reviews describe Class III malocclusion as multifactorial, with inherited and environmental contributions, and trials of facemasks enrolled children with diagnosed Class III bites [14][2].

claims.claim: Homemade facepuller devices can substitute for orthodontic appliances
claims.believers: Members post homemade facepuller builds and helmet-style designs and discuss redesigning the force direction [16][17][18].
claims.experts: No published studies have tested homemade devices. Wikipedia notes eye injuries have been reported with headgear and that safety release straps and safety facebows are used to reduce the risk [1].

claims.claim: Early facemask treatment in children can prevent later jaw surgery
claims.believers: Orthodontic descriptions say early intervention may avoid later surgery [1].
claims.experts: A six-year randomised trial found 36% of treated children versus 66% of controls judged to need surgery [12]; the Cochrane review reports benefits shrinking by three years in one study and uncertain long-term effects [2].

claims.claim: Headgear flattens the face and can reduce airway size
claims.believers: Some patients reported sleep apnea, breathing difficulty and temporomandibular disorder after headgear in the 1980s [1].
claims.experts: A 2006 review reported long-term use may flatten the face and restrict chin growth with reduced SNA and ANB angles; Wikipedia marks the airway link as needing further explanation [1].

claims.claim: A chin cup adds to facemask results after expansion
claims.believers: A thread asks whether to use a chin cup with a facemask after expansion [19].
claims.experts: The 2017 review reports some evidence for the chincup in early Class III treatment, from studies at high risk of bias [11].
